opus-5.5.text:
I think one useful way to look at it is to ask: how recent is the skill, evolutionarily speaking? Take vision, or locomotion, or a kind of basic dexterity. Our ancestors needed those for hundreds of millions of years. So it's quite plausible that evolution has given us an enormous amount of built-in structure there, some prior that's very hard to articulate but very real. When a child learns to walk, or a squirrel jumps between branches, you're not seeing learning from scratch. You're seeing learning on top of a huge foundation.

But then consider things like mathematics, or programming, or chess. These didn't exist until very recently. There's no way evolution could have specifically prepared us for writing code. And yet people learn to code, and some people learn it remarkably well, from what is, compared to what our models see, a tiny amount of data. A teenager can learn to drive in maybe ten hours of practice, and they're reasonably robust. They don't need millions of examples. To me, that's the more telling evidence. When a human is sample-efficient and robust in a domain that evolution could not have anticipated, that suggests something more general: the learning machinery itself is just better, in some way we don't yet fully understand.

There's also the matter of value functions, or something like them. Humans seem to have a very good internal sense of whether they're doing well or badly, even without external feedback. The student learning to drive can tell when they're being clumsy. Some of that might be emotional, and the emotions themselves might be evolutionary, fairly simple and hard-coded, yet still very useful across an incredibly wide range of situations. So you get this interesting picture: a small number of robust, evolutionarily ancient signals, combined with a general learning ability that generalizes far beyond anything those signals were "designed" for.

So my heuristic would be roughly this. If the skill is ancient, be suspicious; a lot of it might be the prior. If the skill is new, and humans still learn it quickly and reliably, that's where you see the general ability. And that second category is, I think, the one that matters most for understanding what our current models are still missing. They generalize much worse than people do, and figuring out why is, in my view, one of the most important questions right now.

r001.rationale: The response says ancient skills such as vision, locomotion, and dexterity may rest on substantial evolutionary priors.

r002.rationale: It describes humans learning recent domains such as programming and chess quickly and robustly, and treats that as evidence of more general learning ability.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think it's actually quite hard to answer cleanly, because evolution has had a very long time to work on us, and so you might expect that almost anything a human does well has some prior behind it.

But here is the way I think about it. Look at the things that humans do that evolution could not possibly have anticipated. Vision, locomotion, recognizing faces, understanding the social dynamics of a small group, those are things where you'd expect the prior to be very strong. We've been doing them for millions of years. A person learns to walk and to see with remarkably little data, in some sense, and that's a hint that a lot of the work was done ahead of time.

Now contrast that with something like mathematics, or programming, or playing a game like Go at a high level. There is no way evolution prepared us specifically for Go. There were no Go boards in the ancestral environment. And yet a person can get quite good at it. Not with the sample efficiency of a child learning to walk, but still, with a few thousand games, a human can become very strong. That's the interesting case. It tells you that whatever is going on inside the brain is not purely a collection of narrow modules. There is some general machinery that can be pointed at a problem it has never encountered before and make real progress.

And I think the honest answer is that it's a mixture, and the mixture is hard to separate. Even when you learn mathematics, you're using representations that evolution gave you, a sense of space, a sense of quantity, language. So the prior is doing something. But the fact that we can go so far beyond what any prior would have specified, that we can learn things that are obviously out of distribution relative to the environment we evolved in, that's what makes me think the general learning component is real and quite powerful.

One more thing I'd add. In machine learning we had this debate for a long time too, about how much needs to be built in versus how much can be learned. And what we've seen over and over is that with enough data and compute, the learned version wins, and often the built-in structure turns out to be a limitation rather than a help. I suspect something similar is true in the brain. The priors matter for sample efficiency, especially early on, but the thing that makes humans interesting is the part that isn't the prior.

r001.rationale: It says skills such as vision, walking, and face recognition were useful over millions of years and likely have strong evolutionary priors.

r002.rationale: It points to learning mathematics, programming, and Go—domains absent from ancestral environments—as evidence of general learning machinery.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: did evolution have an opportunity to select for this particular skill? For something like vision or navigating the physical world, the answer is clearly yes. So when humans learn those things very quickly, it’s hard to know how much to attribute to a general learning algorithm and how much to structure that evolution put there.

But consider mathematics, or programming. Evolution didn’t have an opportunity to select directly for programming ability. Yet people can become very good at it. That suggests that we have learning mechanisms that can be applied to problems far outside the circumstances in which they evolved.

Now, that’s not a clean separation, because programming uses capacities like reasoning and memory that evolution certainly could have selected for. So I wouldn’t say this proves that the brain starts with no useful priors. The interesting thing is that those priors support learning something so different from what our ancestors had to do.

r001.rationale: It says evolution could select for vision and navigating the physical world, making it unclear how much rapid learning in those skills comes from general learning versus evolved structure.

r002.rationale: It contrasts programming and mathematics, which evolution could not select for directly, with people’s ability to become very good at them, suggesting learning mechanisms generalize beyond ancestral circumstances.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s hard to draw a clean line, because evolution could have given us priors that make us good at learning, rather than just priors for particular skills.

But you can look at things that are very far from anything our ancestors would have encountered. Programming is a good example. There was no evolutionary pressure to understand computer programs, and yet people can learn to do it. Mathematics is another example, especially very abstract mathematics. That seems like evidence that we have something quite general.

Now, it’s not a proof. You could say that programming reuses our abilities for language and planning, and those have an evolutionary history. And that’s true. But the ability to reuse those capabilities in a completely new setting is itself part of what you’re trying to explain. So the interesting question is how much evolution put into the specific capabilities, and how much it put into a learning process that can discover new capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response mentions evolutionary priors for particular skills and says language and planning have evolutionary histories, but it does not identify reliable performance in skills useful to ancestors as the relevant evidence.

r002.rationale: It says people can learn programming and abstract mathematics despite these domains being far from what ancestors encountered, and presents this as evidence of a general learning ability.
